step3-grammar.title: Step 3: Grammar, only when you need it

parts.text: Do not study grammar in order. When a sentence blocks you, find the row below, read only that, then go back to the story or conversation.

parts.answer: -are: parlo, parli, parla, parliamo, parlate, parlano. -ere: vendo, vendi, vende, vendiamo, vendete, vendono. -ire: dormo, dormi, dorme, dormiamo, dormite, dormono. Finire adds -isc-: finisco, finisci, finisce, finiamo, finite, finiscono.

essere: sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono · avere: ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno · fare: faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno · andare: vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno · stare: sto, stai, sta, stiamo, state, stanno
-o masculine, -a feminine, -e could be either. Plural: -o → -i, -a → -e, -e → -i. Words ending in an accent (università, città) and loanwords (database) do not change.

parts.when: il / lo / la / l' / i / gli / le
parts.answer: **Masculine:** il (plural i) for most words: il libro, i libri. lo (plural gli) before s + consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y: lo studente, lo zaino, gli studenti. l' (plural gli) before a vowel: l'amico, gli amici. **Feminine:** la (plural le): la casa, le case. l' before a vowel, singular only: l'amica, but the plural is always le: le amiche. Learn each noun with its article.
a, di, in, su, da + il/la merge: al, alla · del, della · nel, nella · sul, sulla · dal, dalla. Plurals: ai, alle, dei, delle, nei, nelle.
avere or essere + participle: ho mangiato, ho studiato · sono andato/a, sono arrivato/a, sono uscito/a (movement verbs take essere).
mi piace + singular, mi piacciono + plural: Mi piace il caffè. Mi piacciono i gelati.
tu with friends, classmates, young people. Lei (verb in 3rd person) with strangers, officials, professors: Parla inglese? Può ripetere?
Ho freddo, ho fame, ho 23 anni. Weather: Fa freddo.

items: **1. Read and listen at once.** Follow the text while the audio plays. Do not stop.
**2. Cognate scan.** Underline every word you recognised from English. You understand more than you think.
**3. Read again, aloud.** Look up at most 5 words. Write whole chunks, not single words.
**4. Retell.** Close it and say what happened in 4–6 sentences. Say it badly; that is the point.

parts.text: After a story section, close the page and say four sentences out loud in Italian about what happened. Speaking aloud matters more than writing. Short and wrong is fine.

parts.title: The four sentences
items: **1. Who and where?** *Sara entra in un bar.*
**2. What does the person want or do?** *Ha sonno e vuole un caffè.*
**3. What happens next?** *Ordina un cappuccino e un cornetto.*
**4. How does it end?** *Paga con la carta ed esce.*

parts.text: Italian writes 1.000 with a dot and 3,50 with a comma. Prices: *tre euro e cinquanta* (3,50 €). Phone numbers are usually said in pairs or single digits: *tre-tre-nove, uno-due...*
Practice: say your age, your phone number, your flat or house number, and the price of a coffee.

parts.text: Months are not capitalised. *a marzo / in marzo* = in March. Dates use a cardinal number, except the first: **il primo ottobre**, **il sette ottobre**. Order is day then month: *Oggi è mercoledì 7 ottobre.* Che data è oggi? (standard) / Quanti ne abbiamo oggi? (informal)

parts.text: Singular family words drop the article after *mio, tuo, suo...*: *mia madre, mio fratello*. Plurals keep it (*i miei genitori, le mie sorelle*), and so does *loro* (*il loro zio*). Boyfriends, girlfriends and friends are not family words, so they keep it (*il mio fidanzato*, *la mia amica*). Careful: *parente* means relative, not parent. More practice: [[res:oic-family-reading|Online Italian Club, a family and hobbies reading exercise]].

parts.title: Family and people, word by word

parts.text: To say what you do, leave out the article: *Sono insegnante. Mio padre è operaio.* Most job names change like other nouns (*cameriere, cameriera*), and these never change: words in *-ista* (*il dentista, la dentista*) and in *-ante* (*l'insegnante*, *il cantante, la cantante*); only the article tells you the gender. Words in *-tore* become *-trice* (*attore, attrice*). Feminine forms of professional titles are debated: *medica* and *dottoressa* are both used, *avvocata* and *avvocatessa* are both accepted (*-essa* can sound ironic for newer titles), and *ingegnera* and *l'ingegnere* are both heard, so the drills accept the common alternatives. More practice: [[res:oic-professions|Online Italian Club, professions]].

items.en: doctor; also a polite title for a university graduate

items.example: Il commesso mi aiuta a scegliere.
Il cassiere mi dà lo scontrino.

parts.text: Most colours agree with the noun: *una casa bianca, due case bianche, un gatto nero, due gatti neri*. Verde has only two forms (*verde, verdi*). Blu, viola, rosa and beige never change (*due macchine blu*). Arancione and marrone take -i in the plural (*marroni, arancioni*), though you will also see them left unchanged, and both are accepted. More practice: [[res:oic-colours|Online Italian Club, colours]].

parts.text: A practical phrasebook for living, studying and getting around in Italy. Phrases keep their original numbers (p001 to p200). Use the polite forms with strangers, landlords and university staff.

parts.title: How to use it
items: Read the Italian first and try to recall the English meaning.
Say each phrase aloud. Audio from a native speaker is best for the exact sound.
Practise 10 to 15 phrases a day and revisit them the next day.
Change one part of a phrase: *Vorrei un caffè* becomes *Vorrei una SIM*.

parts.title: Five flexible patterns to remember
rows: Vorrei un caffè. / Vorrei aprire un conto.

parts.title: Polite or informal
parts.text: Italian distinguishes between speaking informally (tu) and politely (Lei). Use informal wording with friends and classmates once you are comfortable. With a landlord, office staff or someone you do not know, polite forms such as *Mi scusi*, *Parla inglese?*, *Può aiutarmi?* and *Potrebbe spiegarmi meglio?* are safer.

parts.title: Gender agreement
parts.text: Some phrases change with the speaker or the person addressed: *studente / studentessa*, *allergico / allergica*, *perso / persa*, *sicuro / sicura*, *libero / libera*. The notes next to the phrases show the variation.

Rental vocabulary: **deposito cauzionale** is a security deposit that protects the landlord against damage and unpaid rent. A *caparra* is a different thing (earnest money). Ask for the term in writing and read the contract before paying.

parts.title: Emergency
parts.text: In Italy, **112** is the European single emergency number. Use it for urgent emergencies. Official information: [[res:112-gov-it|112.gov.it]].

I'm not sure. (Male speaker; female: sicura)
Are you free today? (To a man; to a woman: libera)
I'll be there in ten minutes.
Would you like to go out? (Can sound like a date invitation.)
How much do I have to pay in total?
When do I have to pay the rent?
Are there other students in the apartment?

items.it: La stanza è disponibile da subito?
Vorrei leggere il contratto prima di firmare.
items.en: I'd like to read the contract before signing.

items.it: Posso visitare la stanza prima di decidere?
items.en: Can I view the room before deciding?

items.it: C'è una fermata dell'autobus nelle vicinanze?
items.en: Is there a bus stop nearby?
Could you send me more photos? (Polite)
I'd like to open a bank account.

items.it: Posso usare il passaporto come documento?
items.en: Can I use my passport as ID?
Do I need a tax identification number?

items.it: Qual è il saldo del mio conto?

items.en: I'd like to withdraw some cash.

items.it: La mia carta è stata rifiutata.

items.en: Can I make an international bank transfer?

items.it: Qual è il tasso di cambio?

pb-sim.title: SIM cards, mobile phones and internet

items.en: I'd like to buy an Italian SIM card.
What plans / offers do you have?
How many gigabytes are included? (Everyday wording)
How much does it cost per month?
I'd like to keep my number.
How can I activate the SIM?

items.it: Non riesco a connettermi al Wi-Fi.
items.en: I can't connect to the Wi-Fi.

items.it: In quale aula si svolge la lezione?
items.en: Which classroom is the lesson in?

items.it: Dove posso trovare l'orario delle lezioni?
items.en: Where can I find the class timetable?
Do you have the lecture notes? (Informal)
Can you explain it to me? (Informal)
When is the exam taking place?
Do we have to work in a group?
I need to speak with the professor. (Female: la professoressa)

items.it: Dove posso trovare il materiale del corso?
items.en: Where can I find the course materials?

items.it: Da quanto tempo ha questi sintomi?
items.en: How long have you had these symptoms? (Polite; a clinician may ask you this)
Do you have something for a cold?

items.it: Dove trovo una farmacia di turno?
items.en: Where can I find a pharmacy that is open on duty / after hours?
I need to make an appointment.
I'm allergic to this medicine. (Male speaker; female: allergica)
Where can I find a doctor?
Could you explain it more clearly? (Polite)
I'd like to resolve this problem.

oic-family-reading.notes: A short text-only reading exercise (true or false statements about a family and its hobbies). No login or payment on the page, no audio. The site also sells online lessons and ebooks (ignore those). Listed in the A1 checklist the owner follows.

oic-professions.title: Online Italian Club - Professions (lesson and exercises)
oic-professions.notes: A lesson page listing common professions with masculine and feminine forms, and two linked exercises (A1 and A2-B1). No login or payment on the page, no audio. The site also sells online lessons and ebooks (ignore those). Listed in the A1 checklist the owner follows.

today.title: Read with audio
today.text: Read one story section while the audio plays. Do not stop at unknown words; underline the cognates you recognise. Then retell it in four sentences.

today.title: Speak out loud
today.text: Review your due cards out loud, then play one scenario. Say it badly; that is the point.
